identification.summary: UTA0178 is Volexity's temporary designation for an unknown actor that Volexity believes is a Chinese nation-state-level actor; it was first seen in December 2023 exploiting two Ivanti Connect Secure zero-days, CVE-2023-46805 (authentication bypass) and CVE-2024-21887 (command injection), chained for unauthenticated remote code execution [S5][S6]. Volexity reported that UTA0178 placed GLASSTOKEN webshells on internal and external-facing web servers, and later GIFTEDVISITOR webshells were found on more than 1,700 compromised appliances as of 14 January 2024 [S5]. The record's existing summary (from Volexity's January 2024 post) describes living-off-the-land behavior in the victim network: pivoting with compromised credentials, harvesting credentials on each new system, and using RDP. That Volexity post could not be opened for this update.
identification.firstObserved: Volexity first detected the intrusion in December 2023 (secondary sources vary between the second week and mid-December; one gives 3 December for first in-the-wild exploitation) [S5][S6][S7].
identification.notes: Name overlap: Mandiant independently tracked the same zero-day exploitation as UNC5221, a suspected espionage actor it said it had not linked to any known group and could not yet assess for origin [S1]. This encyclopedia record lists UNC5221 as an alias; none of the fetched Mandiant/GTIG posts states that UTA0178 equals UNC5221, and the April 2024 Mandiant post does not mention UTA0178 [S1][S2]. Treat the equivalence as an analyst convention pending Volexity's own text. Volexity also reported that other actors, which it tracks separately (named UTA0188 in secondary coverage), had access to the exploit [S5][S8]. Mandiant later reported eight distinct clusters exploiting these CVEs after disclosure [S2]. UNC5221 reporting after 2024 (SPAWN malware, Ivanti EPMM, BRICKSTORM) belongs to the Mandiant/GTIG cluster and is not Volexity-confirmed as UTA0178 activity [S3][S4][S9].

attribution.sponsor: No government attribution in the sources gathered. Volexity assessed that it had reason to believe UTA0178 is a Chinese nation-state-level actor [S5][S6]. Mandiant said for UNC5221 that it had not linked the activity to a known group or enough data to assess origin in January 2024 [S1]; by April 2025 GTIG described UNC5221 as a suspected China-nexus espionage actor [S3].
attribution.confidence: Volexity: belief (not stated as high confidence in the secondary coverage) that the actor is a Chinese nation-state-level actor [S5][S6]. These are vendor assessments, not government attribution.
attribution.basis: Volexity incident response on a customer network in December 2023, and later scanning that found large numbers of compromised appliances [S5]. Mandiant: espionage motivation inferred from targeting and appliance-specific malware [S1]. The basis for Volexity's nation-state judgement is not detailed in the secondary sources reviewed.

objectives: Volexity and Mandiant assessed the activity as consistent with espionage, with credential theft from VPN logons and internal pivoting for access to additional systems [S1][S5]. Mandiant described a subset of high-priority targets for which access was maintained even after patches were released [S1].

sectors: Organizations operating internet-facing Ivanti Connect Secure / Policy Secure gateways (cross-sector) [S1][S5]
Mandiant reported later UNC5221 targeting of legal services, SaaS, BPO and technology firms (BRICKSTORM; GTIG cluster, not confirmed as UTA0178) [S4]
regions: Not specified by Volexity in sources reviewed; Mandiant describes UNC5221 as having targeted a wide range of countries and verticals [S3]
Later BRICKSTORM intrusions were in the United States (GTIG cluster) [S4]
targeting.notes: Early reporting put the number of breached customers under ten, and by 14 January 2024 Volexity identified more than 1,700 compromised appliances, much of that after exploit details spread to other actors [S5][S11]. Victim organizations are not named in the sources reviewed.

capabilities.summary: Volexity: chained CVE-2023-46805 and CVE-2024-21887 for unauthenticated RCE on Ivanti Connect Secure; pulled configuration data, modified files, set up a reverse tunnel, deployed GLASSTOKEN and GIFTEDVISITOR webshells, used proxy utilities, and moved laterally with harvested credentials and RDP [S5][S6]. Mandiant's UNC5221 toolset in the same exploitation: THINSPOOL dropper, LIGHTWIRE and WIREFIRE web shells, WARPWIRE JavaScript credential harvester, and ZIPLINE passive backdoor; the actor remounted the filesystem read/write, trojanized legitimate files, tampered with the Integrity Checker Tool, and used compromised out-of-support Cyberoam appliances as C2 [S1]. Later UNC5221 reporting: SPAWN malware family (SPAWNANT, SPAWNMOLE, SPAWNSNAIL, SPAWNSLOTH), ROOTROT web shell, and BRICKSTORM against VMware vCenter [S2]; TRAILBLAZE and BRUSHFIRE with CVE-2025-22457 [S3]; KrustyLoader and Sliver with Ivanti EPMM CVE-2025-4427/4428 per EclecticIQ [S9]; and BRICKSTEAL and SLAYSTYLE plus bulk mailbox access via Entra ID applications [S4].

campaigns.name: Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day exploitation
campaigns.summary: Volexity detected UTA0178 exploiting CVE-2023-46805 and CVE-2024-21887 on a customer network; Mandiant independently saw UNC5221 exploiting from as early as December 2023 [S1][S5][S6].

campaigns.name: Public disclosure and mass exploitation
campaigns.summary: Ivanti disclosed the flaws and Volexity published; Mandiant published in January 2024. After disclosure other actors exploited the flaws; Volexity counted more than 1,700 appliances with GIFTEDVISITOR by 14 January [S1][S5][S8].

campaigns.name: Mandiant post-exploitation case studies
campaigns.summary: Mandiant described eight clusters exploiting the CVEs; UNC5221 used ROOTROT, moved from an Ivanti appliance to VMware vCenter and deployed BRICKSTORM, and SPAWN malware was tied to UNC5221 (UNC5337 suspected with medium confidence to be UNC5221) [S2].

campaigns.name: CVE-2025-22457 exploitation (UNC5221, GTIG)
campaigns.summary: GTIG attributed exploitation of CVE-2025-22457 and SPAWN deployment to UNC5221, with exploitation observed from mid-March 2025 and disclosure on 3 April 2025 [S3].

campaigns.name: Ivanti EPMM exploitation (UNC5221, EclecticIQ)
campaigns.summary: EclecticIQ, per secondary coverage, attributed exploitation of EPMM CVE-2025-4427 and CVE-2025-4428 to UNC5221 with KrustyLoader and Sliver, hitting healthcare, telecom, aviation, municipal government, finance and defense [S9].

campaigns.name: BRICKSTORM campaign report
campaigns.summary: GTIG attributed BRICKSTORM intrusions since March 2025 against US legal, SaaS, BPO and technology firms to UNC5221 and related clusters, with 393 days average dwell time [S4].

diamond.adversary: Suspected Chinese nation-state-level actor per Volexity (UTA0178); Mandiant's UNC5221 is a suspected China-nexus espionage cluster [S3][S5].
diamond.capability: Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day chain, GLASSTOKEN and GIFTEDVISITOR webshells, credential theft, RDP lateral movement, proxy tools [S5][S6]; Mandiant-observed THINSPOOL, LIGHTWIRE, WIREFIRE, WARPWIRE, ZIPLINE [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Reverse tunnel from compromised appliance (Volexity) [S6]; Mandiant observed compromised out-of-support Cyberoam VPN appliances used as C2 [S1]; later an obfuscation network of compromised Cyberoam, QNAP and ASUS devices [S3].
diamond.victim: Organizations running internet-exposed Ivanti Connect Secure/Policy Secure appliances; downstream internal networks reached by credential theft [S1][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Espionage motivation assessed by Mandiant and consistent with Volexity's nation-state judgement; specific tasking not public [S1][S5].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing VPN edge devices that often lack endpoint monitoring and whose integrity checking can be tampered with [S1][S3].

gaps: Volexity's primary posts (10 and 18 January 2024) could not be opened (host unreachable from the research environment); all UTA0178 detail is from secondary coverage and the record's existing summary [S5][S6][S7][S8].
No source reviewed states that UTA0178 and UNC5221 are the same actor; the alias is inherited from MISP Galaxy. Mandiant's April 2024 post does not mention UTA0178 [S2].

Post-2024 UNC5221 activity (SPAWN, EPMM, BRICKSTORM) is not confirmed as UTA0178; GTIG notes UNC5221 is not the same cluster as Silk Typhoon despite synonymous public use, and GTIG later reportedly renamed UNC5221 as ARMORY CASTLE (search snippet only, not verified) [S4].
Victim names, countries, and sector breakdown for the UTA0178 intrusion are not public in the sources reviewed.
Basis of Volexity's nation-state assessment and any confidence level are not visible in secondary reporting.
Exact first-exploitation date varies among sources (3 December vs mid-December 2023).
No government attribution (CISA, FBI) was reviewed; government sites were not accessed.
Dates for S5, S7, S8, S11 are month-level from search results and were not verified on the pages.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing VPN gateways (Ivanti Connect Secure) are key cyber terrain: they sit on the boundary, hold credentials and often lack endpoint monitoring [S1][S3]. STEP 2: Environment evaluation: exploit details spread within days of disclosure and produced more than 1,700 compromised appliances, so the patch window is short; appliance integrity checking was itself tampered with [S1][S5]. STEP 3: Threat evaluation: zero-day on edge device, webshell, credential harvesting, RDP and credential-driven lateral movement, living off the land [S5][S6]; UNC5221 follow-on includes pivot to VMware vCenter [S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA: continued exploitation of newly disclosed edge-device flaws against unpatched gateways, with persistent credential theft and quiet internal pivoting. MDCOA: pre-disclosure zero-day use against high-value DoD or DIB-adjacent VPNs, with persistence surviving patching and reset [S1][S3]. Candidate indicators: unexpected files on the appliance, ICT failures, new webshell artifacts, unusual outbound connections from VPN appliances, VPN-sourced RDP to internal hosts, and unexpected vCenter VM creation [S1][S2][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: maintain an inventory of edge appliances and their patch/mitigation state and feed vendor integrity-check results to the common operational picture; patch alone is insufficient because the actor persisted past patches [S1][S3]. (2) Authorities: appliance forensics, reset and rebuild for contractor or mission-partner VPNs need clear owner authority; coordinate through the DoD Cyber Crime Center and DIB cybersecurity channels. (3) Mission assurance: plan alternate remote access paths and credential reset procedures, since the actor harvested credentials from VPN logons [S1][S5]. (4) Coordination: multiple clusters exploited the same flaws, so share indicators across partners and avoid single-actor attribution before containment [S2][S8].

provenance.importedSummary: While Volexity largely observed the attacker essentially living off the land, they still deployed a handful of malware files and tools during the course of the incident which primarily consisted of webshells, proxy utilities, and file modifications to allow credential harvesting. Once UTA0178 had access into the network via the ICS VPN appliance, their general approach was to pivot from system to system using compromised credentials. They would then further compromise credentials of users on any new system that was breached, and use these credentials to log into additional systems via RDP. Volexity observed the attacker obtaining credentials in a variety of ways.
